title: Audit Log
markdown:
The audit log is a persistent, searchable, append-only record of what the system did — distinct from episodic memory (which biases future LLM behavior). Every event flows through `audit/logger.log_event`, a synchronous SQLite writer (WAL + 5s busy_timeout) that appends one row to the `audit_log` table in `episodic_memory.db`.

### Event types
Rows are tagged by `event_type`, including `chat_turn`, `specialist_consult`, `tool_invocation`, `scheduled_action`, `alert`, `integration_inbound` (Slack / Discord / email / Telegram / Google Chat), `chat_card_sent` (a card waiting outside any chat sent to its person's chat app with its buttons; ids and channel only, private to that person), plus `knowledge_retrieval`, `content_flagged` (the content check flagged something a chat turn read, naming which item it was, for a mail its subject and sender; private to the person when it was their own mail), `fact_confirmation` (an emailed standing-fact change held, applied, cancelled or refused; private), `fact_reviewed` (the principal approved or declined a teammate's proposed standing fact; private), `fact_approval_changed` (the principal turned "needs my approval" on or off for a teammate; private), `fact_retired` (the principal, or the teammate who recorded it, retired a standing fact from the Pulse page; private, since it names the fact a teammate can no longer read; the fact tools' own rows and their `skill:` dispatch rows are private `tool_invocation` rows, since they quote the principal and name their session and turn), `memory_extraction` (one row per episodic-extraction pass, written in a `finally` so a crashed pass is recorded too: how many items the model proposed, how many were stored, a `{kind, reason}` record per drop, a `malformed` count for payload shapes that were never usable items, and a `failure` naming the exception type when the pass raised — including `CancelledError`, which is a `BaseException` and so would otherwise be logged as a clean empty pass — a `proposed>0, stored=0` streak means the quote validator is rejecting everything, which is otherwise invisible), `cache_event` (one row per model call from every call site — Executive turns, specialist consults (chat turns and workflow steps), research specialists, the research routing and watchlist passes, triage, memory extraction, alert review, the brief's narrative and its grounding repair, the digest, reflection and weekly-review workflows, committee reviewers, and the small utility calls (session titles, the chat-channel response gate, reply parsing, PDF transcription); a unit test fails any model call in the `openexecutive` package that records no row — carrying tokens, cache hits, cost, server-side search count and, inside a research run, its `run_id`), `memory_snapshot`, `committee_review`, `peer_memory`, `attunement` (one row per open-loop extraction pass — opened / closed / dropped with a reason per drop and a `failure` type — plus a row per loop opened or closed and per 👍/👎 on a reply; see Attunement), `executive_paused` / `executive_resumed` (the operator pause switch; actor is the caller's email, details carry the reason, or on resume the held-action count), `scheduled_action_cancelled` (a pending scheduled action cancelled from the Pulse page or a script; actor is the signed-in email, `admin-token` or `local`), `workspace_settings_changed` (solo/team mode, the user's time zone or the principal's role changed through `PUT /workspace`; actor is the caller's email or `api`, details carry the mode's and zone's from/to, plus `role_fields_changed` — the names of the role fields that changed, never their text — when the role changed, and the new `company_domains` list when the company's email domains changed), `decision_class_mode_changed` (a decision class switched between `propose` and `auto_execute` through `PUT /decisions/classes/meeting_scheduling`; same actor rule, details carry the class and the mode's from/to), the Act as me events — `delegation_settings_changed` (a person turned it on or off for themselves), `delegation_reminder_set` and `delegation_reminder_sent` (a person set a reminder for themselves with `remind_me`, and it went to them; ids and times only, never the text; private to that person), `delegation_actions_proposed`, `delegation_actions_approved` and `delegation_actions_dismissed` (the Executive left a person an approval card, which they approved or dismissed; kinds and outcomes only, never the text; private to that person), `delegation_gmail_verified` (their own Gmail checked before turning it on), `delegation_voice_changed` ("How I write" learned, edited, locked or reset, or its signature read from Gmail again), `delegation_voice_described` (a style written from the person's own description, counts only; nothing saved until they save it as an edit), `delegation_drafted` (one per draft saved in their Gmail from chat), `delegation_draft_replaced` (earlier chat drafts deleted from their mailbox because a redraft or the Executive's own send replaced them), `delegation_inbox_changed` (Draft replies to my inbox turned on or off), `delegation_inbox_scanned` (one per inbox scan, with its counts and status), `delegation_reply_drafted` (the inbox watcher saved a reply and made its card), `delegation_reply_dismissed` (a card dismissed, and whether its draft was deleted or kept), `delegation_reply_closed` (a card Gmail already settled: sent or deleted there, answered, gone or expired) and `delegation_reply_sent` (the person tapped Send and the draft went, or the reconciler confirmed an unconfirmed send did) — always private and metadata only: ids, counts and flags, never the draft or the thread; the roster-request events (see Org) — `roster_request_created`, `roster_ack_sent`, `roster_ack_withheld` (an acknowledgement the adapter declined — an email Gmail did not authenticate), `roster_request_resolved` (actor is where it was answered: `web`, a chat channel, `email` or `people_page`), `roster_message_replayed` (one per held message: replayed, dropped, failed or unavailable) and `roster_email_answer_refused` (an emailed answer with no live token, or failing DMARC) — always private to the principal and never carrying what the new sender wrote, like the `integration_outbound` row (`kind: roster_ack`) for the one gateway send allowed to an address off the roster, the fixed acknowledgement; `grounding` (unattended prose that named people or figures its inputs don't hold — a brief or digest that held back lines or used its repair call, a reflection tool call refused or flag held back, a triage or review rewrite replaced; details carry the surface, the mode, the ungrounded names and figures and up to five held-back lines cut to 200 chars, private when the brief read the principal's private rows or the alert is private; in `GROUNDING_CHECKS=report` mode these rows are written and nothing is changed); and the external-signal/monitor events. An unknown chat sender's `integration_inbound` row still reads `rejected_unknown_sender` — it means the message did not reach the Executive, not that it was discarded: a DM or mention is held as a roster request.

### Session & turn context
Each row carries `session_id`, `turn_id`, `actor`, `summary`, `details_json`, `full_json`, `department`, `private_to_principal` and `private_to_person`. A `turn_id` (`f"t-{uuid12}"`) is set per Executive turn and propagated automatically via ContextVars to retriever / specialist / tool / cache emits, grouping one user-assistant exchange. `summary` is the searchable column (LIKE, ~300 char cap); `details_json` is structured and not searched. `department` is filterable in SQL (`AuditLogger.query(department=…)`) — the department check-in's skip rule uses it to ask whether anything was logged for a department since its Goals were last reviewed. A turn another AI app asked over the MCP server and allowed to act runs inside `audit.via_app(name)`: every row it writes gets `details.via`, the client's `clientInfo.name` or "an AI app", and an approval card it proposed keeps `via` on its payload and its approved, handled and held rows (`unscoped_audit_rows` clears it for unattended work started inside).

### Rows private to the principal
The principal reads `/audit`, and others their own rows (see below), so a row about something private to the principal is marked `private_to_principal` as it is written, and only the principal reads it. `AuditLogger.log` marks a row private when its caller passes `private=True` — the email poller's two inbound rows for mail from one of the principal's contacts or mail they forwarded, and `create_alert`'s row for a private alert — or when `people_tools.audit_row_private_to_principal` says so at write time:
- every row a turn private to the principal writes (`Session.private_to_principal`): its reply, each tool call, the model-call rows, and the background passes that inherit the turn;
- on the principal's own verified turn (or inside `grant_contact_egress`), any row whose summary, details or full payload names one of their contacts — their email address or full name anywhere in the text, or their person id or chat id in a person or recipient field (`person_id`, `attendee_person_ids`, `user_id`, `chat_id`, `channel_ref`), JSON tool results included.
- every row an Act as me turn writes once `ghostwrite_email` or a mailbox or calendar read (`search_my_email`, `read_my_email`, `read_my_email_attachment`, `my_email_awaiting_reply`, `my_calendar`) has touched the speaker's mailbox (`TurnDelegation.touched_mail`, set before the tool's first read): the tool row, the reply's `chat_turn` row carrying the draft's preview, the model-call rows, and anything it starts in the background, under `private_rows` (it runs no learning passes). Only the principal can have Act as me for now, so private to the principal is the right visibility; the tool's input and result are also redacted (`ghostwrite`, `my_email` and `my_calendar` are sensitive tool names).
- every row the Act as me inbox watcher, a reply card's Send or Dismiss, an action card's Approve (or the card carried out on its own, in training), or a person's Act as me settings write: they run under `rows_for_person(person_id)` (or pass `private_to_person`), so their model-call rows and events are private, and the reply cards are their own person's alone. That includes a person changing the AI line on replies sent as them (`delegation_disclosure_changed`) or turning Read my calendar on or off (`delegation_calendar_changed`) and what training records: `delegation_training_changed`, `delegation_reply_allowed`, `delegation_example_kept`, `delegation_actions_allowed`, `delegation_actions_handled`, `delegation_actions_held`, `delegation_learned_removed`, and the meeting-invite rows `delegation_invite_carded`, `delegation_invite_answered`, `delegation_invite_handled` and `delegation_invite_dismissed`.

### Rows that belong to one team member
Act as me can be on for team members as well as the principal (see Act as me). What a team member's own mailbox touches must not reach the principal either, so such a row also carries `private_to_person` — the team member's id — as it is written. A teammate's own conversation with the Executive is theirs the same way, as their mail is: every row of a turn a team member other than the principal speaks on a verified surface (the web app signed in, their own Slack or Discord, a secret-verified private Telegram chat) or by email Gmail authenticated as theirs (`people_tools.teammate_turn_owner`), its reply, tool calls, model calls and memory snapshot included. The rows written before the turn binds its session follow the same rule: the chat adapters' `audit_rows_on_senders_turn` holds `rows_for_person` for a verified teammate (`sent_by_teammate`), the web chat route for a signed-in teammate, and the email poller for authenticated teammate mail, which it checks before writing its inbound row. An unproven sender (a forged From, an unverified Telegram chat) keeps the ordinary rule, so nobody can hide a turn from the principal by claiming to be a teammate. `people_tools.audit_row_owner` decides it: the id a caller passes, else the `rows_for_person` scope, else the speaker of a turn whose `touched_mail` is set, else the teammate whose own turn it is; the principal's own id is never stored, so their rows stay private to the principal exactly as above, and a principal lookup that fails keeps the owner. A row with an owner is always private, and `AuditLogger.query` and `count` leave it out in SQL unless the caller asks for that person's rows (`owned_by`; `only_owned` keeps those alone, as the read routes do for a teammate) — so the brief's handled-overnight block and every other internal reader skip it. The read routes show it to the principal as an action only (`api.routes.audit._redact`): the summary is rebuilt from the event type and a plain tool name with whose conversation it was ("mcp:send_gmail_message (Ben's conversation, details private)"), the details keep only what was done and what it cost (`tool`, `kind`, `ok`, `refused`, token counts, …), and `full` is dropped; a text search (`q`) leaves such rows out, so their words never decide a match. The person it belongs to reads it in full. Only `usage_summary` counts it, so spend stays whole. `usage_summary` also adds up the sandboxed scripts (`run_script`) from their own rows — chat's `tool_invocation` with `kind: script` and a workflow step's `workflow_tool_call` with `tool: run_script`, each carrying `calls` and `duration_ms` — into `scripts` (scripts run and worked, tool calls, time, and `turns_avoided`, an upper bound on the model turns those calls would otherwise have needed); a script's individual calls are not counted twice. It also sums the `python_job` rows (one per `run_python_job`: `ok`, `duration_ms`, `cpu_ms`, `peak_mb`, files and bytes in and out, `attachments`, `saved_tool`) into `python_jobs`, with the `cache_event` usage of the turns that ran a job, each turn counted once. Rows that quote someone's own documents follow the same `rows_for_person` scope: a `draft_artifact` / `get_artifact` / `list_artifacts` dispatch row, the document tools' own rows, and a turn's `memory_snapshot` when its retrieval recalled a published document are private to the speaker (to the principal when they are the speaker).

Some rows are written before their turn binds its session, so two scopes in `audit.context` count too. The email poller holds `private_rows` for the whole handling of a mail from a contact or a principal forward: every row is private, the knowledge retrieval (which quotes the mail) included. The chat adapters hold `principal_turn_rows` once they know the principal sent the message on a verified surface (`people_tools.audit_rows_on_senders_turn` on Slack, Discord and Telegram; the web chat route checks its caller), so the inbound row, the knowledge retrieval, alert triage and the start of the web stream follow the principal-turn rule above. Tasks started inside inherit the scope, except unattended work: a workflow run a chat reply resumes and each scheduled action start with neither (`unscoped_audit_rows`), so their rows follow the ordinary rule. A sender lookup that fails counts as not the principal, as the turn's own check does. Neither scope lets the turn reach anyone. A caller can add privacy but never remove it, and a check that cannot run keeps the row private. On anyone else's turn a contact is a stranger, so a row that names one keeps its visibility: hiding it would tell whoever wrote it that the address belongs to a contact. The poller handles each message with no session bound, so one message's private turn never marks the next message's rows.

Every read route resolves the caller as `/alerts` and `/decisions` do (`people.caller_is_principal`: the principal's signed-in email, or no `x-caller-email` — the CLI, direct curl, local login — once a principal is on the roster; before anyone is principal, nobody), in `api.routes.audit._view`. The principal reads every row, a teammate's own as an action only (above). Once a principal is on the roster, anyone else reads their own rows (`owned_by` = them, `only_owned`) and nothing more, since the log holds what everyone said to the Executive; a caller the roster can't resolve reads none. Before anyone is principal, everyone reads the rows not private to one. All of it is filtered in SQL, so `total` and pagination stay honest: `GET /audit/logs` leaves the rest out, `GET /audit/logs/{id}` answers 404 exactly as for a missing id, and `GET /audit/sessions/{id}` shows only the rows the caller reads (404 when none are left). `GET /audit/usage` is spend, not content: for anyone but the principal it leaves out the rows private to the principal, as before. Internal readers see every row unless they ask otherwise; the department check-in, whose report goes to the department, reads its recent activity without them, and its "nothing new since the review" skip rule ignores them too. Ids are one autoincrement sequence, so anyone else can still see a gap where a private row was written; that is accepted.

Always in the loop writes `history_notes_added` (count and source, never the note) and `history_settings_changed`, `history_note_changed`, `history_note_forgotten` and `history_conversation_forgotten` from its routes. Every one is private and belongs to its person alone (`private_to_person`). `recall_history` is a sensitive tool name, so its input and result are redacted.

### Views
- `GET /audit` — filterable list with a "Group by session" toggle and session pills.
- `GET /audit/session/{id}` — full ordered timeline plus a server-derived node/edge graph rendered as a three-pane React Flow chart.

### Invariant
Audit writes never break a chat turn: all writes swallow exceptions and log a warning, and instrumentation observes only — it never touches request building or the cached prompt blocks. Audit is append-only: no UPDATE or DELETE paths exist in product code.
